title: How Bell tests closed their loopholes
summary: You know Bell's inequality: local models give S ≤ 2. Learn how experiments shut the locality and detection escape routes, and why 2015 mattered.
objective: Judge whether a Bell-test design closes the locality and detection loopholes, and say what it would need to close both.

hook.prompt: In early Bell tests, each analyser's angle was set by hand and left alone for the whole run. The results clearly violated Bell's inequality. Why didn't that rule out local hidden variables?

options.text: The settings were known long before each measurement, so a light-speed signal had time to pass them between the stations
The violations were too small to be statistically meaningful
options.feedback: The violations were clear. The problem was the design: no amount of data fixes a gap a local model can slip through.

options.text: Quantum mechanics predicts no violation for photons, so the results were suspect
options.feedback: Quantum mechanics does predict a violation for entangled photons, and the results matched it. The question is whether a local model could match it too.

hook.explanation: With settings fixed for minutes, a local influence had ages to carry one side's setting to the other. The fix: choose settings while the particles are in flight.

bricks.title: Locality: beat the light signal
bricks.body: A local hidden-variable model may let one station's setting influence the other's outcome, but no faster than light. To rule that out, each station picks its setting **at random, fresh for every pair**, and the other station must finish its readout before light from that choice could arrive. For stations \(L\) apart, that window is \(L/c\): about 40 ns for 12 m, 1.3 µs for 400 m. Settings fixed in advance, or following a pattern, leave the loophole open.

term.definition: Two events so far apart in space, and so close in time, that no signal at light speed or slower can link them.

visual.alt: Spacetime diagram: a pair flies from a central source to stations A and B; A picks its setting, and B must finish its readout before light from that choice reaches B.

bricks.prompt: Two stations sit 300 m apart, so light needs 1 µs to cross. Which design closes the locality loophole?

options.text: A fast random generator picks each pair's settings in flight; each station's readout ends within 0.5 µs of the other's choice
A random generator picks the settings at the start of each one-second run
options.feedback: Random, but not fresh per pair. A setting fixed for a second gives a light-speed signal a million microseconds to cross 300 m.

options.text: Settings switch every 10 ns in a repeating pattern, as in Aspect's 1982 test
options.feedback: Fast enough, but predictable: a local model could know each future setting from the pattern, so it needn't send any signal at all.

options.text: Move the stations 300 km apart and keep the settings fixed for the run
options.feedback: Distance only helps if the settings are chosen late. Fixed settings are known before the pairs even leave the source.

bricks.hint: Check two things: is each setting unpredictable, and is it chosen inside the 1 µs window?
bricks.explanation: Each setting is unpredictable and chosen per pair, and 0.5 µs fits inside the 1 µs light window, so no light-speed influence links one side's choice to the other's outcome.

bricks.prompt: Delft's 2015 stations were about 1.3 km apart, with the entangling source between them. How long could each station take, from setting choice to finished readout, and still close the locality loophole?

options.text: About 4.3 µs
About 2.2 µs
options.feedback: That's light time from the middle to one station. The window is set by the distance between the two stations, since that's how far the signal must travel.

options.text: About 8.7 µs
options.feedback: That's a round trip. The signal only has to get from one station's choice to the other station once.

options.text: About 4.3 ms
options.feedback: Right method, wrong unit. Light covers 1.3 km in microseconds, not milliseconds.

bricks.hint: Which distance does a signal from one station's choice have to cover?
bricks.explanation:
The window is L/c, with L the distance between stations.
1,300 m ÷ 300,000,000 m/s ≈ 0.0000043 s
= 4.3 µs

bricks.title: Detection: count the pairs you missed
bricks.body: Photon tests used to detect only a small share of pairs and assumed those were a **fair sample**. A local model can exploit that: each particle carries instructions like "at this setting, don't click", so the counted pairs skew towards ones that fit the quantum pattern, and the clicks violate the inequality while the full set wouldn't. Without that assumption, efficiency must beat a threshold: about 82.8% for CHSH with maximally entangled pairs, or 2/3 with Eberhard's less-entangled pairs.

term.definition: Assuming the detected pairs behave like all the pairs emitted, so the undetected ones can be ignored.

visual.alt: A 0 to 100% detection-efficiency scale with two thresholds marked: Eberhard's 66.7% and CHSH's 82.8%.

bricks.prompt: A photon Bell test detects 20% of pairs and finds S = 2.7 among them, with enormous statistical significance. A colleague says local hidden variables are ruled out. What's the strongest objection?

options.text: A local model could reach S = 2.7 among detected pairs by controlling which pairs go undetected
S = 2.7 is above the quantum limit, so the data must be faulty
options.feedback: The quantum limit is 2√2, about 2.83, so 2.7 is allowed. The issue is which pairs were counted.

options.text: Nothing: with that significance, the 80% missed pairs don't matter
options.feedback: Significance rules out chance, not bias. If the missed pairs aren't a fair sample, more data just measures the skew more precisely.

options.text: The stations should be farther apart
options.feedback: That's the locality loophole. Even perfect spacelike separation leaves the 80% of missing pairs unexplained.

bricks.explanation: At 20% efficiency, far below either threshold, the result leans on fair sampling. A local model with "don't click" instructions can produce exactly this.

bricks.prompt: Each setup violated Bell's inequality. Which loophole does each one leave open?

items.text: Two trapped ions a few micrometres apart, read out almost perfectly
Two superconducting qubits on one chip, read out in every trial
Photons with 75%-efficient detectors and Eberhard's states, settings changed slowly in one lab
Photons 400 m apart, fast random settings, a few percent of pairs detected
Photons 144 km apart between two islands, random settings, most pairs lost
Photons 12 km apart through fibre, random settings in flight, detectors catching 10% of pairs

bricks.hint: For each one, ask: is the window L/c beaten, and is efficiency above the threshold?
bricks.explanation: Close-together systems with near-perfect readout fail on locality. Distant photons with fast random settings but low efficiency fail on detection. Each closes only one.

bricks.prompt: The 2013–2015 photon experiments deliberately used pairs that were less than maximally entangled. Why?

options.text: To lower the detection efficiency needed from about 83% to about 67%
To get a bigger violation of the inequality
options.feedback: With perfect detectors, maximally entangled pairs give the biggest violation. Less entanglement trades violation size for tolerance of missed pairs.

options.text: To make the locality window longer
options.feedback: The window is L/c; it depends on distance, not on the state. This choice is about the detection loophole.

options.text: Less-entangled pairs need no fair-sampling assumption at any efficiency
options.feedback: Close: they lower the bar, but don't remove it. Below about 2/3 efficiency, a local model can still exploit the missed pairs.

bricks.hint: Which threshold could real photon detectors actually reach?
bricks.explanation: Detectors at around 75% are below 82.8% but above 2/3, so Eberhard's less-entangled states made a detection-loophole-free photon test possible.

bricks.title: Both at once: the 2015 tests
bricks.body: A local model needs only one open loophole, and before 2015 every test left one. That year, three teams closed both in a single run, with fast random settings inside the \(L/c\) window. Delft **heralded** its pairs: entangled electron spins 1.3 km apart, a signal flagging each ready pair, and every flagged trial read out. Photons lost on the way just meant no flag, whatever the settings. Vienna and NIST used photons with superconducting detectors above Eberhard's threshold.

term.definition: A separate signal that announces each entangled pair before measurement, so every announced trial is counted, whatever its result.

bricks.prompt: In Delft's test, nearly all the photons sent to the heralding station were lost. Why didn't that reopen the detection loophole?

options.text: A lost photon only meant no flag, regardless of the settings, and every flagged trial got a measured outcome
The 1.3 km distance made the losses irrelevant
options.feedback: Distance closes the locality loophole. Losses are a detection question, and distance doesn't answer it.

options.text: The team assumed the lost photons were a fair sample
options.feedback: That's exactly the assumption a loophole-free test must avoid. Heralding is what let Delft drop it.

options.text: Their photon detectors were above the 82.8% threshold
options.feedback: The thresholds apply to the particles being measured. Here those were the spins, and every flagged pair's spins were read out.

bricks.hint: Can a missed photon at the heralding station depend on a setting?
bricks.explanation: Losses only decided whether a trial started, independent of the settings. Once flagged, no trial could drop out, so there was nothing for a local model to filter.

bricks.prompt: A hypothetical team heralds entangled atoms in labs 400 m apart, reads out every heralded trial, and picks settings at random. Each station needs 2 µs from setting choice to finished readout. What's still open?

options.text: The locality loophole
The detection loophole
options.feedback: Heralding plus reading out every heralded trial closes it, as at Delft. Check the timing instead.

options.text: Nothing: it's loophole-free
options.feedback: Detection is closed, but compare 2 µs with the light time for 400 m.

options.text: Both loopholes
options.feedback: Heralding with full readout closes detection. Only one is open here.

bricks.explanation: 400 m ÷ 300,000,000 m/s ≈ 1.3 µs. A 2 µs readout lets light from one side's choice arrive before the other side finishes.

challenge.situation: You're designing a photon Bell test between two labs 60 m apart, so light needs 200 ns to cross. Each station picks a random setting and finishes its readout within 150 ns. Your detectors catch 60% of photons, and you use Eberhard's less-entangled pairs.

options.text: Keep the layout and upgrade to superconducting detectors well above 2/3 efficiency.
options.outcome: 150 ns already fits inside the 200 ns window, so locality was closed. The detector upgrade closes detection too: a loophole-free design.

options.text: Upgrade the detectors and move the labs 1 km apart to be safe.
options.outcome: It can work, but the move wasn't needed, and a longer fibre loses more photons, eating into the efficiency margin you just paid for.

options.text: Move the labs 1 km apart; 60% is close enough to the threshold.
options.outcome: Locality was already closed. At 60%, below Eberhard's 2/3, a local model can still fake the result with "don't click" instructions.

options.text: Run ten times longer so the violation is overwhelmingly significant.
options.outcome: More data measures the skewed sample more precisely. It doesn't close either loophole.

challenge.explanation: Check both: 150 ns is inside the 200 ns window, so locality holds; 60% is below 2/3, so detection is open. Fix only the detectors.

takeaways: To close locality, choose each setting at random per pair and finish the other side's readout within L/c of that choice.
To close detection, beat the efficiency threshold (82.8%, or 2/3 with Eberhard's states) or herald every trial; never lean on fair sampling.
A test is loophole-free only when it closes both in the same run, as Delft, Vienna and NIST did in 2015.
